summary:
Malawi criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, and the law reaches gender identity directly through its application to people whose gender expression departs from expectations. Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 remain in force. Human Rights Watch records that men face up to fourteen years' imprisonment and women five years under sections 153 and 156, and the sections were before the courts in 2024 as carrying up to fourteen years.

On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court rejected the challenge to those sections. The application had been brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The court left any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the decision a dark day and warned that it exposes LGBT people to heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.

Faith-based groups filed briefs in the proceedings, and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming that the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage.

Enforcement is documented as arbitrary and accompanied by violence. Human Rights Watch's 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge', published on 26 October 2018 and based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and in some cases assaulted them in custody. The report concludes that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are most likely to be targeted.

Detention routinely draws community and police abuse. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 on homosexuality charges had their house ransacked by neighbours, were assaulted, and were threatened with being burned alive; they also faced attempted extortion and humiliation by community police, including forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photographs of them distributed on social media.

The suspension of arrests has itself been contested. A 2012 moratorium on arrests issued by the justice minister was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after litigation by religious leaders, leaving its legality contested. In April 2018 police in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, an apparent attempt to circumvent the six-year moratorium while both provisions faced a constitutional challenge; police spokespersons confirmed his custody.

Healthcare carries its own exposure. The 2018 Human Rights Watch report records medical staff denying services on grounds of gender expression, including a trans man who was beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses who mocked people presenting for HIV tests.

Documents and family law offer no route out. The sources describe no process for legal gender recognition. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, states that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender.

Malawi has no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The only nationwide protection identified is narrow and dates from 2019: sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d) of the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019 bar broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference.

Hostility has been voiced at the highest levels of the state. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage "evil and bad before the eyes of God"; in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, saying he would "hunt you in your homes... smoke you out", and both went into hiding amid treason threats. A 2011 United States State Department report found that senior officials created a discriminatory environment, citing tourism minister Daniel Liwimbi describing same-sex activity as "very un-Malawian". In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda wrote on Facebook that gay people "are worse than dogs" and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges, but the director of public prosecution took over the matter and discontinued it on 21 January. In February 2014 the Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people, and on 4 January 2017 thousands marched across 28 districts against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi.

Proceedings and public statements against individuals show how quickly visibility becomes a legal event. In 2010 Peter Sawali was arrested and sentenced to 60 days for posting "Gay rights are human rights" posters in Blantyre. Bail was denied to Tiwonge Chimbalanga and Monjeza in 2009 because "the public out there is angry with them", and the magistrate said he sentenced them to protect society. In January 2016 an interview in which gay man Eric Sambisa said "Kill us or give us our rights" led to his brief police detention and a period in hiding. International media coverage of the 2009 trial failed to report Tiwonge Chimbalanga's gender identity.

International protection machinery has produced statements but no change in the statute. At the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the Malawi government rejected every recommendation to decriminalise same-sex relations, saying it "had no plans to legalize homosexuality" and that it "should not be unduly singled out and unnecessarily pressured"; recommendations had come from Sweden, Mexico, France, Canada, Germany, Australia, the United Kingdom, Italy, Austria, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United States, Spain, Switzerland and Norway. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence, and Malawi has not filed its ICCPR report for over 17 years.
tangentialFactors:
Malawi is described in its own 2012 UN report as a highly conservative country in which "the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and homosexuality is not practiced in the open". That framing is offered by the government itself rather than by outside observers.

Public anger has previously produced lethal outcomes. The United States State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi documents the July 2011 protest killings, in which 20 people died, alongside harsh prison conditions and "discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons".

Official rhetoric against LGBT people has sometimes crossed into direct intimidation of named individuals, as with the 2011 threats against Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence, and into incitement that the justice system declined to pursue, as with the Msonda charges discontinued on 21 January 2016. The pattern differs from jurisdictions where senior officials are constrained by anti-incitement enforcement.

Aid conditionality is a live domestic political issue. The Malawi Council of Churches urged international organisations to "refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise sinful acts like homosexuality", and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid. HIV funding for LGBT services has been contrasted with official hostility: in September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued that Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services on a human rights basis, and CEDEP's Gift Trapence has set that funding against the treatment of arrested LGBT people.

Visibility is emerging but fragile. The country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with more than 50 attendees delivering a petition for marriage equality and healthcare, and a June 2021 petition to Lilongwe city officials demanded better healthcare access for LGBTQ people. Neither event is matched by any change in the penal code or in family law.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156 as they stand after the Constitutional Court's judgment of 28 June 2024, with reform in the hands of parliament. The court's dismissal of the challenge means the exposure to imprisonment is current law, not a suspended or repealed provision.

Marriage is closed. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans same-sex marriages and unions, assigns gender at birth for the purposes of the statute, and bars a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery from marrying someone of that person's prior gender. No process of legal gender recognition exists, so identity documents continue to reflect birth-assigned gender.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity has no general legal remedy. The narrow exception is the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d), which constrain broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of gender identity or sexual preference; the regulations do not reach speech in other media or conduct by employers, clinics or schools.

Practical exposure in encounters with the state remains high. Police have been recorded arresting and detaining transgender people arbitrarily and assaulting them in custody, and the December 2015 arrests show community police using forced stripping, forced HIV/STD examinations and social-media distribution of images as punishment. Charging decisions have been shaped by attempts to work around the moratorium, as in April 2018.

Healthcare is not a safe setting for gender-nonconforming people. Documented refusals of treatment and mockery by nurses at HIV testing points mean that seeking routine or emergency care can itself disclose gender history and invite denial of service.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced: the current legal status of the 2012 moratorium on arrests. It was suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation and its legality was described as contested at that point; the inventory contains no later ruling, appeal or reinstatement.

Not sourced: any parliamentary action on the Penal Code after the Constitutional Court's judgment of 28 June 2024, and whether a reform bill has been introduced, debated or defeated.

Not sourced: entry, visa and border-document rules as they apply to travellers whose passports carry a gender marker inconsistent with presentation. The inventory contains nothing on immigration screening, airport questioning, or consular assistance to detained trans nationals, so visitor-facing entry risk is not established either way.

Not sourced: current enforcement statistics, the number of arrests under sections 153, 154 and 156 in the years since 2018, and whether trans visitors rather than residents have been prosecuted. Available evidence on arrests concerns residents and dates from 2015 to 2018.

Not sourced: the specific penalty attached to section 154. The inventory gives the fourteen-year maximum for sections 153 and 156 collectively and the five-year figure for women under sections 153 and 156, but no separate range for section 154.

Several claims here rest on a single secondary compilation of country coverage rather than a primary legal text or court record, including the wording of the Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, the citations to the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, and the account of the 2011 Universal Periodic Review exchanges. Those provisions should be verified against the gazetted instruments and the official review record before they are relied on individually. Prison conditions and the treatment of the 2021 sentence given to Jana Gonani beyond the fact of her eight-year term in a men's prison are also not documented in the inventory.
